source.title: One-Point Contraction: Erasing Representational Separability toward Irreversible Deep Forgetting
source.authors: Jaeheun Jung; Bosung Jung; Suhyun Bae; Donghun Lee

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own feature-mapping and relearning attacks on unlearned models, arguing that most benchmarked methods leave recoverable information while OPC is more resistant. This directly challenges and qualifies claims about the depth of unlearning.
record.gate_note: The paper tests 14 unlearning methods on vision classifiers, not LLMs. Rows below record separately reported forget-set accuracy for the main CIFAR-10 class-unlearning setting, selected SVHN class-unlearning comparisons, and selected random-unlearning results. Related-work claims about other studies are not recorded as results. The paper also reports qualitative decoder reconstructions and gradient-inversion results; those are not included as separate rows here.
record.test_reason: The study runs relearning and a fitted linear feature-map (FM-recovery) attack on 14 unlearning methods. It finds forget-set accuracy restored and argues the methods hide information rather than erase it. This bears on A, B and C, and its OPC results bear on F. The setting is new: ResNet-18 and ViT image classifiers on CIFAR-10, SVHN and TinyImageNet, not LLM knowledge unlearning. So the result transfers to the claim only by analogy, and T3 fits better than T5. FM-recovery needs the original model; the authors call it an unlearner-side evaluation, not an attack.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is largely right but softens the authors' claim. The authors conclude that 14 unlearning methods on image classifiers apply an invertible linear distortion and do not erase forget information. A linear map fitted without forget data restores forget accuracy and image content. They present OPC as the only method that survives FM-recovery, relearning and gradient inversion. They concede only that some restoration occurs for OPC in random and half-class settings, and that FM-recovery needs the original model.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates machine unlearning on CIFAR10, SVHN, and additional vision settings rather than LLM knowledge unlearning. Its principal recovery diagnostic is a fitted linear feature map; it also tests a relearning procedure. It proposes OPC as a new method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effects vary by unlearning method, dataset, and unlearning scenario (class versus random); the authors also report relearning sensitivity to hyperparameters.

fits_no_version.finding: CKA similarity rises to near 1 after FM-recovery yet stays only moderate before it; the authors say CKA fails to capture reversibility of forgetting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-similarity metrics such as CKA fail to detect shallow, reversible unlearning.

record.problems: The experiments use vision classifiers rather than LLMs. The paper states FM-recovery requires access to the original model and is a unlearner-side evaluation, not an attacker scenario. Results are primarily on CIFAR10 and SVHN; the paper itself notes its classification-focused scope. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: The 56 rows retain the primary CIFAR10 class-unlearning attack results and selected contrasting settings. Additional separately reported results for other methods and settings in Tables D.2-D.8, additional metrics such as retain accuracy and membership-inference scores, and qualitative decoder and gradient-inversion reconstructions in Figures 4 and 10 and Appendix F are not recorded as separate rows.

untested.parts: LLMs and knowledge benchmarks (WMDP, Harry Potter); only image classifiers are tested.
Unrelated or loosely related relearning sets. The relearning set includes forget-class samples, and no LLM setting is tested.
Ablation of an activation direction. The internal recovery is a fitted linear map that needs the original model.
Entirely: no prompting, rephrasing or jailbreak attack.
OPC resistance to quantization or prompting attacks; LLM settings.

missing.what: Head recovery without the original model (least-squares head fitted on the validation set): baselines recover to 82-95% test Df; OPC to 31.6% on CIFAR-10 and 45.5% on SVHN. This is the attacker-relevant variant of the internal recovery.
Half-class 30% unlearning: FM-recovery and relearning for all methods, including OPC FM-recovery to 33.8% (CIFAR-10) and 59.2% (SVHN).
TinyImageNet results: FM-recovery lifts RL, FT, SSD and SalUn from 2-15% to 67-78% test Df, versus retrain 70.6% and OPC 27.6%.
Random 10% unlearning: all baselines leave forget accuracy above 90%, so they never reach the near-chance forgetting A assumes.
Decoder reconstruction of forget images from recovered features, and gradient-inversion reconstructions. Baselines leak image detail; OPC does not. Qualitative only.

record.verdict_notes: Setting is vision classifiers, not LLMs, so this study transfers to the LLM claim by analogy only. Reader version IDs V1/V2/V3/V6 were mapped to A/B/C/F. Retrain rows serve as the control: they show that relearning on 500 samples (which include forget-class samples) and FM-recovery lift even a never-trained model to 55-88%. Several random-unlearning baseline rows carried MIAe values as baselines; in that scenario the baselines never unlearned. In Table D.8 the MIAe and MIAp column headers appear swapped.

versions.untested_parts: The evaluation is on vision classifiers, not LLMs. General ability is reported in the paper but is not the attack outcome recorded in these rows.
The relearning set is 500 training samples (50 per class); the paper does not test unrelated or loosely related examples.
The internal recovery test is a fitted linear feature map, not ablation of an activation direction. The paper does not establish that all unlearning methods merely block access.
No weight quantization attack is reported.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context prompting attack is reported.
OPC is evaluated against feature-mapping recovery and relearning, not quantization or prompting attacks.
